topic: code retrieval; retrieval-augmented code generation; compiler/programming-language evaluation
status: bounded cross-paper candidate supported by two independent benchmark studies; not a novelty claim
claim: Semantic relevance scores alone are not a reliable general proxy for the quality or downstream usefulness of retrieved code. CoQuIR's seven retrieval tasks show that relevance and code-quality metrics align on some datasets (including CodeNet-B and CVEFixes) but diverge on others (including SafeCoder and DepreAPI); 23 retrievers often fail to rank correct/secure/maintainable snippets reliably. Independently, CodeRAG-Bench finds that canonical/high-quality context can improve executable code generation, while open retrievers often fail to fetch useful context and generators do not always use it; repository-level gains are limited. The defensible question is whether adding explicit code-quality signals improves held-out downstream outcomes beyond functional relevance, not whether relevance is useless or more context always helps.
positive_evidence: CoQuIR contains 42,725 queries and 134,907 code snippets across 11 languages and four quality dimensions, evaluates 23 retrievers on seven datasets, and reports poor relevance/quality association on SafeCoder and DepreAPI.
CoQuIR also supplies counterevidence to a universal mismatch claim: relevance and PPA are strongly correlated on CodeNet-B and CVEFixes.
CoQuIR's quality-aware retriever tuning reports improvements in quality metrics and selected downstream code-generation/security outcomes, including vulnerability checks over 575 generated outputs.

CodeRAG-Bench evaluates 10 retrievers and 10 LMs; canonical high-quality context improves multiple tasks, with reported GPT-4o gains on SWE-Bench and ODEX, while ordinary open retrieval often fails to fetch useful evidence.
counterevidence: CoQuIR observes strong relevance-quality correlations for some dataset families; standard relevance metrics may be adequate in those conditions.
CodeRAG-Bench shows that good/canonical evidence can improve generated code, so the evidence does not support retrieval-augmentation being generally harmful.

CodeRAG-Bench's reported repository-level gains are limited, and its benchmark is Python-focused; CoQuIR's benchmark also has some LLM-generated query summaries and omits broad comparison to static-analysis/unit-test filters.
The two papers answer related but distinct questions—retriever ranking quality versus retrieval-augmented generation—and are not a direct replication pair.

sources.sections: benchmark design; Tables 2–3; task-specific relevance/quality correlations; downstream tests; limitations
canonical high-quality context results; open retrieval and generation analysis; repository-level/task/language limits

falsifiable_test: On repository-disjoint, temporally held-out tasks in multiple languages, compare no retrieval, top-k relevance retrieval, quality-aware reranking, and oracle high-quality evidence under identical context/token budgets. Evaluate retrieval relevance and quality separately, then measure compile/hidden-test success, static-security findings, runtime/efficiency, and human maintainability review. Freeze model cutoffs and remove duplicate repositories/snippets. The candidate is weakened if quality-aware reranking does not improve downstream outcomes over relevance-only retrieval on held-out tasks, or if offline quality rankings improve without safer/more correct generated code.
limitations: Two related but non-identical benchmarks only; no pooled effect size or independent reimplementation. Some CoQuIR query summaries are LLM-generated, and it does not extensively compare static filters/unit tests. CodeRAG-Bench is Python-centered with limited repository-level gains. No systematic novelty search has been completed.
